propositions.text: This is an appeal from the Federal Court dismissing judicial review of a Trade-marks Opposition Board interlocutory decision.
propositions.quote: This is an appeal from a decision of the Federal Court, reported as 2015 FC 980, dismissing an application for judicial review of an interlocutory decision of a member of the Trade-marks Opposition Board (the Board) under the delegated authority of the Registrar of Trade-marks.

propositions.text: The Board dismissed McDowell's request to amend her statement of opposition to Automatic Princess's trade-mark application.
propositions.quote: The Board dismissed the appellant Heather Ruth McDowell’s (McDowell) request to amend her statement of opposition to the respondent Automatic Princess Holdings, LLC’s (Automatic Princess) application to register a trade-mark.

propositions.text: The Federal Court dismissed judicial review because no special circumstances justified reviewing an interlocutory decision.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court dismissed the application for judicial review on the basis that there were no special circumstances that would justify reviewing an interlocutory decision.

propositions.text: The Federal Court found McDowell had an adequate alternate remedy via other Trade-marks Act proceedings.
propositions.quote: In particular, the Federal Court found that McDowell had an adequate alternate remedy in the form of other proceedings under the Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985 c. T-13 (the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains this appeal arises from the Federal Court dismissing judicial review of the Board's interlocutory decision denying McDowell's amendment request, finding no special circumstances and an adequate alternate remedy.

propositions.text: There is conflicting Federal Court case law on what constitutes an adequate alternate remedy for interlocutory decisions in trade-mark opposition.
propositions.quote: There are conflicting decisions of the Federal Court as to what constitutes an adequate alternate remedy in the context of interlocutory decisions in trade-mark opposition proceedings.

propositions.text: This appeal offers an opportunity to resolve the conflict and the appeal is allowed for reasons below.
propositions.quote: This appeal provides an opportunity to resolve this conflict. For the reasons set out below, I would allow the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes conflicting Federal Court decisions on adequate alternate remedies and states it will allow the appeal to resolve this conflict.

propositions.text: McDowell applied to register the HONEY trade-mark in 2002 and HONEY & DESIGN in 2003.
propositions.quote: In 2002, McDowell applied to register the HONEY trade-mark; in 2003, she applied to register the HONEY & DESIGN trade-mark.

paragraphs.summary: McDowell applied to register the HONEY and HONEY & DESIGN trade-marks in 2002 and 2003 respectively.

propositions.text: Automatic Princess applied to register HONEY B. FLY in 2003; it was approved and advertised in 2009.
propositions.quote: In 2003, Automatic Princess applied to register the trade-mark HONEY B. FLY. In 2009, the trade-mark was approved and advertised in the Trade-marks Journal.

paragraphs.summary: Automatic Princess applied for HONEY B. FLY in 2003, approved and advertised in 2009.

propositions.text: McDowell filed a statement of opposition in 2010 based on non-entitlement and non-distinctiveness, not pleading paragraph 12(1)(d).
propositions.quote: On May 3, 2010, McDowell filed a statement of opposition opposing Automatic Princess’ application. The statement of opposition was based on non-entitlement and non-distinctiveness. It did not plead or refer to paragraph 12(1)(d) of the Act, which provides that a trade-mark is not registrable if it is confusing with a registered trade-mark.

paragraphs.summary: McDowell opposed Automatic Princess's application in 2010 on non-entitlement and non-distinctiveness, omitting paragraph 12(1)(d).

propositions.text: McDowell's HONEY and HONEY & DESIGN trade-marks were registered on May 18, 2010.
propositions.quote: On May 18, 2010, HONEY and HONEY & DESIGN were registered as trade-marks.

paragraphs.summary: McDowell's HONEY and HONEY & DESIGN trade-marks were registered in May 2010.

propositions.text: Automatic Princess filed a counter-statement in July 2010; McDowell filed Anastacio's affidavit including registrations.
propositions.quote: In July 2010, Automatic Princess filed a counter-statement. In November 2010, McDowell filed the affidavit of Elenita Anastacio, which included the registrations for the HONEY and HONEY & DESIGN trade-marks.

propositions.text: Registrations were issued after McDowell's opposition; Anastacio was cross-examined but not on registrations.
propositions.quote: As can be seen from the chronology above, the registration of the marks was issued after McDowell filed her statement of opposition. Ms. Anastacio was cross-examined on her affidavit but was not asked any questions about the trade-mark registrations that were exhibits to her affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: Automatic Princess filed a counter-statement; McDowell filed Anastacio's affidavit with registrations, but cross-examination did not address registrations.

propositions.text: Automatic Princess filed affidavit in 2013; McDowell declined written argument and requested oral hearing in 2014; Automatic Princess filed written argument and requested oral hearing.
propositions.quote: Automatic Princess filed its own affidavit in 2013. In March 2014, McDowell indicated that she would not file written argument and asked for an oral hearing. Automatic Princess filed its written argument in July 2014 and also requested an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Automatic Princess filed affidavit in 2013; McDowell requested oral hearing without written argument; Automatic Princess filed written argument and requested oral hearing.

propositions.text: McDowell's counsel requested leave to amend statement of opposition to include registrations and paragraph 12(1)(d).
propositions.quote: On August 14, 2014, counsel on her behalf wrote to the Board requesting leave to file an amended statement of opposition.

propositions.text: Original opposition included pending applications and indicated registration was imminent; registrations attached to Anastacio affidavit.
propositions.quote: The original statement of opposition included copies of the pending applications for McDowell’s trade-marks and indicated that both had been allowed and that registration was therefore imminent. Copies of the registrations of McDowell’s trade-marks were attached as exhibits to the Anastacio affidavit.

propositions.text: Automatic Princess was aware of registrations and chose not to cross-examine on them; no prejudice would result from amendment.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding the fact that the registrations were put into evidence, no questions about them were asked when Anastacio was cross-examined on her affidavit. In the circumstances, counsel of Automatic Princess should be taken to have been aware of the existence of the registrations and to have chosen not to cross-examine Anastacio with respect to those registrations. As a result, Automatic Princess would suffer no prejudice if the amendment were allowed, but McDowell was prepared to consent to reasonable measures to allow the former to amend its argument to reflect the fact of the registrations and to respond to arguments based on paragraph 12(1)(d) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: McDowell's counsel requested leave to amend opposition to include registrations and paragraph 12(1)(d), arguing Automatic Princess knew of registrations and would suffer no prejudice.

propositions.text: The Board rejected McDowell's amendment request due to late stage, probable reading of respondent's argument, and inadvertence explanation.
propositions.quote: The Board rejected McDowell’s application for leave to amend her statement of opposition. It noted that the application was made at a very late stage in the proceedings, probably after having read Automatic Princess’ written argument. The Board also noted the absence of an explanation for the failure to plead the registrations other than inadvertence.

propositions.text: The amendment was important as it added a ground not requiring evidence of use.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the amendment was of some importance since it added a ground of opposition that does not require McDowell to lead evidence of use of her trade-marks.

paragraphs.summary: The Board rejected McDowell's amendment request due to lateness, inadvertence, and importance of the new ground.

propositions.text: The Board found Automatic Princess would be prejudiced by amendment as it would allow case splitting, not in interests of justice.
propositions.quote: The Board was of the view that Automatic Princess would be prejudiced by the amendment as it would allow McDowell to split her case, which was not in the interests of justice.

propositions.text: The Board applied factors from Part VII of its procedure manual in dismissing the amendment application.
propositions.quote: With that in mind, and having regard to the factors set out in Part VII of Practice in Trade-mark Opposition Proceedings (the Board’s procedure manual), the application to amend the statement of opposition was dismissed.

propositions.text: The Board had already referred to these factors in its decision.
propositions.quote: The factors in Part VII are the ones to which the Board had already referred in its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Board found prejudice from amendment due to case splitting and dismissed the application applying Part VII factors from its manual.

propositions.text: An application to have the Board reconsider its decision was also dismissed.
propositions.quote: An application to have the Board reconsider its decision was also dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The Board also dismissed the reconsideration application.

propositions.text: Federal Court considered whether to judicially review interlocutory decision, citing Szczecka and C.B. Powell.
propositions.quote: After setting out the facts, the Federal Court turned to the threshold issue of whether it should entertain a judicial review of an interlocutory decision. Citing this Court’s decisions in Szczecka v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 116 D.L.R. (4th) 333, 25 Imm. L.R. (2d) 70 (F.C.A.)[Szczecka] and C.B. Powell Ltd. v. Canada (Border Services Agency), 2010 FCA 61, [2011] 2 F.C.R. 332 [C.B. Powell], the Federal Court held that, in the absence of special circumstances, a reviewing court should not judicially review interlocutory decisions.

propositions.text: One special circumstance justifying review is absence of an adequate alternative remedy.
propositions.quote: One special circumstance among others is the absence of an adequate alternative remedy.

propositions.text: There is conflicting Federal Court jurisprudence on whether refusal to amend a statement of opposition has an adequate alternate remedy.
propositions.quote: This led to a consideration of the conflicting jurisprudence in the Federal Court. While the Federal Court cases are consistent on the need for special circumstances, they differ on whether there is an adequate alternate remedy in the case of a refusal to permit an amendment to a statement of opposition.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court held interlocutory decisions are not judicially reviewed absent special circumstances, including lack of adequate alternate remedy, noting conflicting case law on amendment refusals.

propositions.text: In Parmalat, Federal Court found no right of appeal from dismissal of amendment application, so no remedy within Board proceedings.
propositions.quote: In Parmalat Canada Inc. v. Sysco Corporations, 2008 FC 1104, 69 C.P.R. (4th) 349 [Parmalat] the Federal Court noted that, on the authority of McDonald’s Corp. v. Coffee Hut Stores Ltd., 55 C.P.R. (3d) 463, 76 F.T.R. 281 (F.C.) [McDonald’s], there is no right of appeal from the dismissal of an application to amend a statement of opposition.

propositions.text: This lack of remedy was a special circumstance justifying judicial review of interlocutory amendment dismissal.
propositions.quote: This was found to be a special circumstance that justified judicial review of an interlocutory decision dismissing an application to amend a statement of opposition.

paragraphs.summary: Parmalat found no appeal right from amendment dismissal, constituting special circumstance justifying judicial review.

propositions.text: McDonald's authority appears doubtful but was not challenged, so its correctness is left for future determination.
propositions.quote: I might add that it appears to me that McDonald’s is a doubtful authority. However, given that it was not challenged, I leave the question of its correctness to be determined when it arises.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds McDonald's authority doubtful but leaves its correctness for future consideration.

propositions.text: In Dairy Processors, remedies outside Registrar proceedings were not adequate alternate remedies under Szczecka and C.B. Powell.
propositions.quote: In the decision below, the Federal Court noted that in Dairy Processors Association of Canada v. Dairy Farmers of Canada, 2014 FC 1054, 128 C.P.R. (4th) 393 [Dairy Processors], the Court found that the availability of remedies other than in administrative proceedings before the Registrar was not an adequate alternative remedy as contemplated by Szczecka and C.B. Powell because those procedures occurred outside the framework of the original proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: Dairy Processors held remedies outside Registrar proceedings are not adequate alternate remedies under Szczecka and C.B. Powell.

propositions.text: In Indigo, Federal Court held adequate alternate remedy existed because aggrieved party could start other proceedings outside opposition seeking expungement.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, in Indigo Books & Music Inc. v. C. & J. Clark International Ltd., 2010 FC 859, 86 C.P.R. (4th) 349 [Indigo], the Federal Court held that there was an adequate alternate remedy due to the fact that the aggrieved party could commence other proceedings, outside the framework of the opposition proceedings, seeking a remedy such as expungement.

propositions.text: Therefore, no special circumstances justified Federal Court intervention in Indigo.
propositions.quote: As a result, there were no special circumstances justifying the Federal Court’s intervention.

paragraphs.summary: Indigo held adequate alternate remedy existed via other proceedings, so no special circumstances justified intervention.

propositions.text: C.B. Powell discourages interlocutory judicial review to avoid fragmenting process and costs, especially if underlying proceeding may succeed.
propositions.quote: Citing C.B. Powell, the Federal Court commented that its disinclination to intervene in interlocutory proceedings avoids fragmenting the administrative process and eliminates the costs and delays associated with interlocutory judicial review, particularly when the applicant for judicial review may be successful in the underlying proceeding in any event.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court cited C.B. Powell to discourage interlocutory judicial review to avoid fragmentation and costs, especially if underlying case may succeed.

propositions.text: Federal Court distinguished Parmalat and Dairy Processors as involving amendments not properly subject to opposition proceedings.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court distinguished Parmalat and Dairy Processors, saying that the amendments sought to be introduced in those cases raised issues that were not properly the subject of opposition proceedings.

propositions.text: Federal Court was concerned about case splitting and found Indigo's reasoning more persuasive than Parmalat or Dairy Processors.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court also expressed its concern with respect to parties splitting their cases. It found the reasoning in Indigo more persuasive than that in Parmalat or Dairy Processors.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court distinguished Parmalat and Dairy Processors, concerned about case splitting, and preferred Indigo's reasoning.

propositions.text: Federal Court found no special factors justified intervention and dismissed judicial review application.
propositions.quote: In the end, the Federal Court found that there were no special factors justifying the Court’s intervention with respect to the Board’s interlocutory decision and dismissed the application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court concluded no special factors justified intervention and dismissed judicial review application.

propositions.text: Does McDowell have an adequate alternate remedy such that her judicial review application should be dismissed?
propositions.quote: Does McDowell have an adequate alternate remedy such that her application for judicial review should be dismissed?

propositions.text: If not, is the Board’s decision reasonable?
propositions.quote: If not, is the Board’s decision reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issues: whether McDowell has an adequate alternate remedy to dismiss judicial review, and if not, whether the Board's decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Federal Court jurisprudence debates what constitutes an adequate alternate remedy.
propositions.quote: The debate in the Federal Court jurisprudence centres on the question of what constitutes an adequate alternate remedy.

propositions.text: In Dairy Producers and Parmalat, an adequate alternate remedy must be available within the administrative process itself.
propositions.quote: In Dairy Producers and Parmalat, the Federal Court held that an adequate alternate remedy must be one that is available within the administrative process itself

propositions.text: In Indigo, another proceeding leading to the same result was found to be an adequate alternate remedy.
propositions.quote: while in Indigo, it found that another proceeding that could lead to the same result was an adequate alternate remedy.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Federal Court cases differ on adequate alternate remedy: Dairy Producers requires administrative process remedy; Indigo allows other proceedings.

propositions.text: C.B. Powell held that the administrative process is established by Parliament and courts are not part of it.
propositions.quote: Under the Act, Parliament has established an administrative process of adjudications and appeals in this area... The courts are no part of this.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites C.B. Powell that Parliament created an administrative process excluding courts from involvement before completion.

propositions.text: Courts can only proceed after all adequate administrative remedies are exhausted.
propositions.quote: The normal rule is that parties can proceed to the court system only after all adequate remedial recourses in the administrative process have been exhausted.

propositions.text: This rule is well-established in Canadian administrative law with many Supreme Court decisions.
propositions.quote: The importance of this rule in Canadian administrative law is well-demonstrated by the large number of decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada on point

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the rule that courts intervene only after exhausting administrative remedies, supported by Supreme Court decisions.

propositions.text: Recourse to courts before exhausting administrative remedies is unjustified and not ambiguous.
propositions.quote: It is clear from these passages that recourse to the courts before the remedies provided in the administrative process have been exhausted is not justified. There is no ambiguity on this point.

propositions.text: A different proceeding under a different statute producing the same result does not engage adequate alternate remedy doctrine.
propositions.quote: The fact that a different proceeding, pursuant to a different statutory provision, might produce the same result does not engage the doctrine of adequate alternate remedy.

propositions.text: The objective is to avoid fragmenting administrative processes that provide review, not to force litigants into different proceedings.
propositions.quote: The objective is to avoid fragmenting administrative processes that already provide for a form of review. It is not to force litigants into different proceedings to obtain redress.

propositions.text: Indigo was wrongly decided and should not be followed.
propositions.quote: As a result, it is my view that Indigo was wrongly decided and ought not to be followed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes that courts should not intervene before exhausting administrative remedies, rejects Indigo, and aims to avoid fragmenting processes.

propositions.text: Federal Court confused adequate alternate remedy and prematurity doctrines.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court appears to have confused adequate alternate remedy and prematurity.

propositions.text: Adequate alternate remedy is part of prematurity doctrine but they address different issues.
propositions.quote: The doctrine of adequate alternate remedy comes within the broader doctrine of prematurity, but they are not the same.

propositions.text: Adequate alternate remedy respects Parliament's administrative scheme; prematurity prevents delay by premature court recourse.
propositions.quote: Adequate alternate remedy deals with the case of respecting the administrative scheme created by Parliament... Prematurity deals with preventing parties from delaying proceedings by coming to court for a remedy that may prove to be moot or overtaken

propositions.text: Prematurity is best understood in interlocutory decision context.
propositions.quote: Prematurity is best understood in the context of interlocutory decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Federal Court confused adequate alternate remedy with prematurity, explaining their distinct roles and contexts.

propositions.text: Neither adequate alternate remedy nor prematurity doctrines apply here because no administrative review of Board's decision is provided.
propositions.quote: In this case, neither the doctrine of adequate alternate remedy nor that of prematurity is applicable. This is not a case where the legislation provides for an administrative review of the Board’s decision.

propositions.text: Dismissal of amendment application means Board will not address paragraph 12(1)(d), so McDowell cannot get relief from Board.
propositions.quote: As for prematurity, the dismissal of the application to amend the statement of opposition means that the Board will not deal with the issue of paragraph 12(1)(d) in its final decision. As a result, there is no possibility that McDowell will obtain the relief she seeks from the Board.

propositions.text: Therefore, judicial review application is not premature.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the application for judicial review is not premature.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds neither doctrine applies; no administrative review exists, Board won't address key issue, so judicial review is not premature.

propositions.text: Federal Court erred in law by dismissing judicial review for adequate alternate remedy.
propositions.quote: As a result, I am of the view that the Federal Court erred in law when it dismissed the application for judicial review on the basis that McDowell had an adequate alternate remedy.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds the Federal Court erred in dismissing judicial review on adequate alternate remedy grounds.

propositions.text: First step in appellate review is determining the standard of review.
propositions.quote: The first step in appellate review is the determination of the standard of review.

propositions.text: This Court must decide if Federal Court chose and applied the correct standard of review.
propositions.quote: When this Court hears an appeal from the Federal Court sitting as a court of review, it must decide if the Federal Court chose the appropriate standard of review and applied it correctly

propositions.text: This Court steps into Federal Court's shoes and focuses on underlying administrative decision.
propositions.quote: In practical terms, this means that this Court steps into the shoes of the Federal Court and focuses on the underlying administrative decision

paragraphs.summary: The court explains appellate review requires deciding if Federal Court applied correct standard, focusing on underlying administrative decision.

propositions.text: Standard of review for specialized tribunals is presumed reasonableness, barring exceptions not relevant here.
propositions.quote: The standard of review of specialized administrative tribunals is presumed to be reasonableness, subject to certain exceptions that are not relevant to this case

propositions.text: Presumption of reasonableness has not been rebutted here.
propositions.quote: The presumption of reasonableness has not been rebutted here, nor could it be.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is presumed reasonableness and that presumption stands here.

propositions.text: Board's reasons for refusing amendment do not withstand critical scrutiny.
propositions.quote: The reasons given by the Board for its refusal to allow McDowell to amend her statement of opposition do not, with respect, withstand critical scrutiny.

propositions.text: Board noted amendment was late, probably after reading Automatic Princess’ written argument.
propositions.quote: The Board noted that the application to amend was made late in the proceedings, probably after having read Automatic Princess’ written argument.

propositions.text: Board was concerned amendment would allow McDowell to split her case to Automatic Princess’ prejudice.
propositions.quote: The Board was also concerned that allowing the amendment would allow McDowell to split her case, to Automatic Princess’ prejudice.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Board's refusal reasons weak; Board cited lateness and prejudice concerns from case splitting.

propositions.text: Amendment was late, especially after Automatic Princess filed written argument, but delay-caused prejudice can be remedied by extra time.
propositions.quote: It is true that the amendment was sought late in the proceeding; in particular, it was sought after Automatic Princess had filed its written argument. This is a factor to be considered but where any prejudice caused by the delay can be remedied by allowing the other party additional time, it ought not be a determinative factor.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges amendment was late but says prejudice can be remedied by granting more time, so lateness alone is not decisive.

propositions.text: Permitting amendment would not allow McDowell to split her case; it aims to consider all issues.
propositions.quote: It is difficult to understand how permitting the amendment would allow McDowell to split her case.

propositions.text: McDowell was not seeking advantage by forcing Automatic Princess to commit without full facts.
propositions.quote: McDowell was not seeking to gain some advantage by forcing Automatic Princess to commit itself to a position without knowledge of all the material facts.

propositions.text: Registrations were exhibits to Anastacio affidavit; Automatic Princess had notice and likely knew of omission before McDowell.
propositions.quote: The registrations were included as exhibits to the Anastacio affidavit. Automatic Princess had notice of the registrations and was likely aware of McDowell’s omission before she was.

propositions.text: Any prejudice to Automatic Princess can be remedied by giving it time to take necessary steps for fairness.
propositions.quote: Any prejudice to Automatic Princess can be remedied by giving it time to take such steps as the Board deems necessary to achieve fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds amendment would not split the case; Automatic Princess had notice; any prejudice can be remedied by extra time.

propositions.text: Board's statement that inadvertence alone is not an explanation is not understandable.
propositions.quote: It is also difficult to understand the Board’s statement that no explanation other than inadvertence was offered for the failure to plead the registrations and paragraph 12(1)(d) of the Act.

propositions.text: Inadvertence is a fact of life and McDowell’s counsel explained circumstances; no reason to disbelieve explanation.
propositions.quote: Inadvertence is a fact of life and while we all hope to avoid missteps due to inadvertence, we are not always successful. McDowell’s counsel explained the circumstances leading to the application. There was no reason to disbelieve the explanation he gave.

paragraphs.summary: The court cannot understand Board's rejection of inadvertence as explanation; counsel's explanation was credible.

propositions.text: Board failed to consider significant factor: long delay in dealing with Automatic Princess’ registration application.
propositions.quote: A further consideration in assessing the reasonableness of the Board’s decision is the fact that it failed to consider a significant factor that ought to have led it to allow the amendment, namely the long delay in dealing with Automatic Princess’ application for registration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Board unreasonably failed to consider the long delay in Automatic Princess’ registration application.

propositions.text: Automatic Princess applied to register trademark in 2003; approved and advertised only in 2009.
propositions.quote: Automatic Princess applied to register its trade-mark in 2003. For reasons that are not apparent, it was not approved and advertised until 2009.

propositions.text: McDowell filed opposition in 2010; Automatic Princess filed affidavit in 2013; omission discovered in 2014; no further progress.
propositions.quote: McDowell filed her statement of opposition in 2010 and her supporting affidavit later that year. Automatic Princess filed its affidavit in 2013. The inadvertent failure to plead the registration of McDowell’s trade-marks was discovered in 2014. On the record before us, it appears that matters have not proceeded any further since then.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts timeline: 2003 application, 2009 approval, 2010 opposition, 2013 affidavit, 2014 omission found, no progress since.

propositions.text: In 2017, Automatic Princess’ registration application still pending after 14 years.
propositions.quote: We are now in 2017 and Automatic Princess’ application for registration is still pending, as far as I can tell on the record before us.

propositions.text: 14-year delay calls for out-of-the-ordinary measures.
propositions.quote: A 14-year delay calls for out-of-the-ordinary measures.

propositions.text: McDowell might succeed without relying on registrations and paragraph 12(1)(d), but may not.
propositions.quote: It may be that McDowell could succeed in her opposition without having to rely on her registrations and paragraph 12(1)(d) of the Act; but she may not.

propositions.text: If not, McDowell may continue opposing by expungement proceedings, prolonging uncertainty over marks and registrability.
propositions.quote: In that case, McDowell would have an incentive to continue to oppose Automatic Princess’ use of its mark, perhaps by launching expungement proceedings. This would simply prolong the uncertainty over Automatic Princess’ marks and their registrability.

propositions.text: This prolonged uncertainty is not in the interests of justice.
propositions.quote: This is not in the interests of justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the 14-year delay and risk of prolonged uncertainty if McDowell must continue opposing, which is unjust.

propositions.text: Given extraordinary delays, Board should have assisted parties to move matter forward.
propositions.quote: Given the extraordinary delays in this case, it was incumbent on the Board to assist the parties in moving this matter forward.

propositions.text: Board’s failure to do so makes its decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Board’s failure to do so is another factor that made its decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Board unreasonably failed to assist parties amid extraordinary delays, making its decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: Board’s reasons for refusing amendment do not meet transparency and intelligibility criteria from Dunsmuir.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I am of the view that the Board’s reasons for refusing McDowell’s application for an amendment do not satisfy the criteria of transparency and intelligibility: Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at paras. 47-48

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Board’s refusal reasons lack transparency and intelligibility as required by Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: Set aside Federal Court’s judgment with costs here and below.
propositions.quote: I would therefore set aside the Federal Court’s judgment with costs here and below.

propositions.text: Return matter to Board with direction to allow McDowell’s amendment application on terms necessary to do justice.
propositions.quote: I would return the matter to the Trade-marks Opposition Board with a direction that McDowell’s application to amend her statement of opposition is to be allowed on such terms as are necessary to do justice between the parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court sets aside Federal Court judgment and remands to Board to allow McDowell’s amendment application with just terms.
